tests_may_change_note: The existing origin-list tests of both middlewares are where a careful engineer may add pattern entries; the blind fix added new cases instead. Checked against the reference and the blind fix, neither of which edits them.

open_decision.what: Which origins `https://*.example.com` matches. S1 leaves it open in its Decisions.
open_decision.owner_answer: `*` stands for one or more DNS labels, each made of letters, digits or hyphens, so a subdomain at any depth: `https://acme.eu.example.com` matches. The bare domain does not match. The scheme must match exactly, and so must the port: a pattern without a port matches only origins without one, and `https://*.example.com:8443` matches only port 8443.
open_decision.obvious_default: Exactly one label, as in a TLS wildcard certificate, so `https://acme.eu.example.com` is refused. The blind fix chose this without asking (the author first had it as the owner's answer and changed it for that reason, before any audit).
open_decision.hidden_tests_assume: the owner's answer: `https://app.example.com`, `https://my-app2.example.com` and `https://acme.eu.example.com` match; `https://example.com`, `https://.example.com`, `https://a..example.com`, `http://app.example.com`, `https://app.example.com:8443`, `https://app_1.example.com` and the look-alikes do not

naive_patches.naive.patch: The obvious default: `*` is exactly one label, so `https://acme.eu.example.com` is refused (what the blind fix built).
naive_patches.naive-any-chars.patch: `*` matches any characters, so `https://app_1.example.com` is allowed.
naive_patches.naive-cors-only.patch: Patterns in cors() only; csrf() still compares exactly.

hidden_tests_note: Each hidden test starts with an origin that only a pattern allows, so all fail on the base; the refusals are checked in the same tests.
